title: Sometimes It Is Good to Interfere
content: As any first-year physics student can remind you, the resolution of photon microscopy is limited by the diffraction of light. Because light travels as waves, an infinitely small point of light cannot be focused to a similar small point; rather, it can only be focused to a small spherical spot, the Airy disk. The size of the Airy disk varies depending on the wavelength of the light, the refractive index of the imaging media, and the angular aperture of image collection. This limits the standard resolution of a microscope using visible light to about 200nm. Below that limit, the information is blurred. However, over the past two decades, biological microscopists have come up with very creative ways to tease out additional information about cell structure and use this information to predict what is happening within the blur. In this way they can partially correct the blurring. These methods, providing corrected resolutions below the 200nm limit, fall under the heading of nanoscopy techniques, with some “super resolution” techniques achieving resolutions in the 20nm range [1].
